```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  prompt = FALSE
)
library(readjsa)

fixture <- function(name) {
  installed <- system.file("extdata", name, package = "readjsa")
  candidates <- c(
    installed,
    file.path("..", "inst", "extdata", name),
    file.path("inst", "extdata", name)
  )
  path <- candidates[nzchar(candidates) & file.exists(candidates)]
  if (!length(path)) stop("The packaged fixture is missing: ", name)
  path[[1L]]
}

ivi_path <- fixture("ivi_skill_states.xlsx")
reos_path <- fixture("reos_current.xlsx")
salm_path <- fixture("salm_sa2.csv")
```

`readjsa` provides a small, explicit surface for three official publication
families from Jobs and Skills Australia (JSA) and the Department of
Employment and Workplace Relations (DEWR): the Internet Vacancy Index (IVI),
the Recruitment Experiences and Outlook Survey (REOS), and Small Area Labour
Markets (SALM). The package has two complementary paths:

* `read_ivi()`, `read_reos()`, and `read_salm()` discover a current official
  release, download it over HTTPS, verify it, cache the exact bytes, and parse
  it.
* `read_ivi_file()`, `read_reos_file()`, and `read_salm_file()` parse one
  local workbook or CSV with the same schema checks. The local path is the
  deterministic choice for a report, a test, or an offline environment.

This article begins with the second path, then replays the first path from a
pinned official workbook. The files directly under `inst/extdata/` are small,
deterministic **schema fixtures** maintained for package examples and tests;
they are not extracts of current production observations. The separate
`inst/extdata/official/` directory contains the provenance-documented official
snapshot used for the chart.

## Parse one file from each family

The first successful workflow is to locate a packaged fixture and pass it to
the family-specific local reader. A family must be supplied for IVI because a
release contains multiple workbook layouts. SALM requires a geography, and
REOS can select one or more workbook tables.

```{r parse-fixtures}
ivi <- read_ivi_file(ivi_path, family = "skill_states")
reos <- read_reos_file(reos_path, tables = c("1.1", "3.3"))
salm <- read_salm_file(salm_path, geography = "sa2")

data.frame(
  dataset = c("IVI", "REOS", "SALM"),
  rows = c(nrow(ivi), nrow(reos), nrow(salm)),
  first_date = c(min(ivi$date), min(reos$date), min(salm$date)),
  last_date = c(max(ivi$date), max(reos$date), max(salm$date)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
```

Each result is a base `data.frame`. Observation columns are followed by
family metadata such as classification and workbook/file notes, then by the
provenance columns repeated on every row. The common fields
`date`, `value`, `observation_status`, and `raw_value` make it possible to
write family-independent checks, while fields such as `occupation_code`,
`table`, or `data_item` retain the source-specific dimensions.

```{r inspect-output}
ivi[c(
  "date", "value", "observation_status", "series_type",
  "occupation_title", "state", "family_id", "source_filename"
)]
```

Dates are returned as `Date` values. Numeric values are canonicalised to
`value`, and the unmodified token is retained in `raw_value`. A status other
than `"published"` is meaningful: for example, SALM uses
`"unavailable"` for a publisher dash and `"not_published"` for `n.p.`. The
parser does not silently turn those publication states into ordinary zeros.

```{r status-example}
salm[salm$observation_status != "published", c(
  "date", "geography_code", "data_item", "value",
  "observation_status", "raw_value"
)]
```

REOS percentages are represented as decimal proportions (for example,
`0.50`, not `50`). The `unit` and `unit_multiplier` columns make that choice
explicit and are retained alongside the source labels.

```{r reos-contract}
reos[c("table", "date", "value", "unit", "frequency", "seasonal_adjustment")]
```

## Retrieve and chart a time series

For a current release, discover the IVI catalogue, select the skill-level/state
workbook, retrieve it through `read_ivi()`, and use ordinary base subsetting to
prepare the chart data.

```{r official-time-series-live, eval=FALSE}
catalogue <- discover_jsa_releases("ivi")
release <- catalogue[catalogue$family_id == "skill_states", , drop = FALSE]
ivi <- read_ivi(tables = "skill_states", release = release)

chart_data <- ivi[
  ivi$series_type == "trend" &
    ivi$measure == "online_job_advertisements" &
    ivi$skill_level == "0" &
    ivi$observation_status == "published" &
    ivi$state %in% c("NSW", "VIC", "QLD") &
    ivi$date >= as.Date("2019-01-01"),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]
```

The rendered figure uses the installed June 2026 JSA workbook so the article
builds without network access. This is a pinned snapshot, not the current
publisher release: 440,452 bytes, SHA-256
`5bacad1cf2fbef22b1f802e3fc3d8c5051038c31ff5839a2af7e8db10e8185fd`,
released 22 July 2026. Attribution is © Commonwealth of Australia; reuse is
CC BY 4.0 subject to the publisher's stated exclusions. The hidden setup below
uses the same public discover/select/fetch/cache/parse path with a local
copying transport.

```{r official-time-series-replay, include=FALSE}
official_snapshot_name <- "ivi_skill_states_2026-06.xlsx"
official_snapshot <- fixture(file.path("official", official_snapshot_name))
ivi_html <- fixture("ivi.html")

official_catalogue <- discover_jsa_releases("ivi", html = ivi_html)
official_release <- official_catalogue[
  official_catalogue$family_id == "skill_states", , drop = FALSE
]
stopifnot(nrow(official_release) == 1L)

transport_calls <- 0L
snapshot_transport <- function(url, destination, timeout, max_bytes) {
  transport_calls <<- transport_calls + 1L
  bytes <- file.info(official_snapshot)$size
  stopifnot(!is.na(bytes), bytes > 0, bytes <= max_bytes)
  stopifnot(file.copy(official_snapshot, destination, overwrite = TRUE))
  invisible(url)
}

chart_cache <- tempfile("readjsa-official-cache-")
first_read <- read_ivi(
  tables = "skill_states",
  release = official_release,
  cache_dir = chart_cache,
  transport = snapshot_transport
)
ivi <- read_ivi(
  tables = "skill_states",
  release = official_release,
  cache_dir = chart_cache,
  transport = snapshot_transport
)
stopifnot(
  identical(transport_calls, 1L),
  identical(first_read, ivi)
)
unlink(chart_cache, recursive = TRUE)

chart_data <- ivi[
  ivi$series_type == "trend" &
    ivi$measure == "online_job_advertisements" &
    ivi$skill_level == "0" &
    ivi$observation_status == "published" &
    ivi$state %in% c("NSW", "VIC", "QLD") &
    ivi$date >= as.Date("2019-01-01"),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]
stopifnot(
  nrow(chart_data) > 0L,
  inherits(chart_data$date, "Date"),
  is.numeric(chart_data$value),
  !anyDuplicated(chart_data[c("date", "state")]),
  all(chart_data$state %in% c("NSW", "VIC", "QLD")),
  all(chart_data$series_type == "trend"),
  all(chart_data$skill_level == "0"),
  all(chart_data$observation_status == "published")
)

snapshot_metadata <- unique(chart_data[
  ,
  c(
    "source_url", "terms_url", "raw_sha256", "raw_bytes", "release_date",
    "licence", "attribution"
  ),
  drop = FALSE
])
stopifnot(
  nrow(snapshot_metadata) == 1L,
  identical(
    snapshot_metadata$raw_sha256[[1L]],
    "5bacad1cf2fbef22b1f802e3fc3d8c5051038c31ff5839a2af7e8db10e8185fd"
  ),
  identical(as.numeric(snapshot_metadata$raw_bytes[[1L]]), 440452),
  identical(as.character(snapshot_metadata$release_date[[1L]]), "2026-07-22"),
  identical(
    snapshot_metadata$licence[[1L]],
    "CC BY 4.0 subject to stated exclusions"
  ),
  identical(snapshot_metadata$attribution[[1L]], "© Commonwealth of Australia")
)
```

The plot can now use the returned `date`, `value`, and `state` columns directly.

```{r official-time-series-chart, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.8, fig.align="center", out.width="100%", fig.alt="Monthly Internet Vacancy Index trend for New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland from January 2019 to June 2026"}
if (requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  print(
    ggplot2::ggplot(
      chart_data,
      ggplot2::aes(x = date, y = value, colour = state)
    ) +
      ggplot2::geom_line() +
      ggplot2::labs(
        title = "Internet Vacancy Index trend by state",
        subtitle = "Monthly published observations",
        x = "Month",
        y = "Online job advertisements",
        colour = "State or territory",
        caption = "Source: Jobs and Skills Australia, Internet Vacancy Index."
      ) +
      ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
  )
}
```

The parsed data retain the exact source URL, terms URL, hash, byte count,
release date, licence, and attribution used to verify the rendered snapshot.
For live work, use the visible retrieval code above; the local transport is
only a deterministic documentation safeguard.

## Read current releases when network access is available

The network-enabled readers are intentionally explicit about their source
families. For example, `read_ivi("skill_states")` discovers the official IVI
catalogue and then reads that family; `read_reos(tables = c("1.1", "3.3"))`
selects workbook tables; and `read_salm("sa2")` selects the SA2 release. These
calls require HTTPS access to the publisher pages and files, and can create
or reuse the package cache. They are not run in this vignette so that the
article remains deterministic and safe to build offline.

For a reproducible analysis, persist the release catalogue row and the
`raw_sha256` value returned in the provenance columns. For a fully offline
workflow, retain the downloaded file and use the corresponding `*_file()`
reader as shown above.

## What to check next

Before analysing values, check the family-specific identifiers and the
provenance fields. In particular:

* IVI `series_type`, occupation fields, and geography fields describe the
  workbook sheet that was parsed.
* REOS `table`, `series`, `disaggregation_group`, and `disaggregation` retain
  the workbook metadata needed to interpret a percentage.
* SALM `classification_version` records the ASGS vintage stated by the file,
  and `file_notes` retains the publisher's availability note.

All three readers validate the expected schema and raise an error when a file
is missing, malformed, or no longer matches the supported publication shape.
The [source families](source-families.html) article shows how to inspect the
catalogue and choose among the supported layouts; the
[reproducibility and cache](reproducibility-and-cache.html) article shows an
offline cache replay; and [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.html) demonstrates
the main failure classes.
